title: What Protestants deny: the perfection of the law strictly taken
source_text: XXXVIII. Id solum igitur in hac quaestione Protestantes negare intendunt, fideles per Christi spiritum renovatos legem implere posse, secundum totam illam perfectionem, quam lex rigide sumpta, ab homine exigit. Porro lex rigide sumitur quum aestimatur ex prima sua institutione, & spectatur quatenus primo homini lata fuit, & continet primum illud foedus cum homine initum, ex cujus observatione perennem & beatam vitam, a Dei bonitate & justitia simul expectare debebat. Lex autem sic considerata exigebat ab homine perpetuam obedientiam, nullis peccatis interruptam, nec ullis defectibus, & naevis obscuratam, & per quam homo cum summa alacritate, absque ulla pugna, vel renitentia affectuum internorum, in omnibus omnino, sine exceptione, sese voluntati divinae submitteret. Qualem, scilicet, obedientiam primi nostri parentes, in statu innocentiae, Deo exhibere poterant, & exhibere reapse tenebantur, ut in beato illo statu manerent, & tandem aeterna cum Deo felicitate fruerentur.
pass_a_gloss: XXXVIII. This alone therefore in this question do the Protestants intend to deny, that the faithful renewed through the spirit of Christ can fulfil the law, according to all that perfection, which the law taken strictly, demands from man. Now the law is taken strictly when it is assessed from its first institution, & is regarded so far as it was given to the first man, & contains that first covenant made with man, from the observance of which he was to expect perpetual & blessed life, from the goodness & justice of God together. But the law so considered demanded from man a perpetual obedience, interrupted by no sins, nor obscured by any defects, & blemishes, & through which man with the highest readiness, without any struggle, or resistance of the inward affections, in absolutely all things, without exception, would submit himself to the divine will. Such, namely, an obedience as our first parents, in the state of innocence, were able to show to God, & were actually bound to show, that they might remain in that blessed state, & at length enjoy eternal happiness with God.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXVIII. The one thing Protestants mean to deny in this question, then, is that believers renewed by Christ's Spirit can fulfil the law with the whole perfection that the law, strictly taken, demands of man.

The law is taken strictly when it is judged by its first institution: as it was given to the first man and contained the first covenant made with him, by keeping which he was to look for unending and blessed life from God's goodness and justice together.

Taken in that way, the law demanded of man a perpetual obedience, broken by no sins and darkened by no defects or flaws, in which he would submit himself to God's will with the utmost readiness, with no struggle or resistance of the inner affections, in absolutely everything and without exception. This was the obedience our first parents could give God in the state of innocence, and were actually bound to give, so that they might remain in that blessed state and at last enjoy eternal happiness with God.
